profiles.meeting_scenario: A troubleshooting meeting at a digital health startup piloting an IoT-enabled decision support system for type-2 diabetes monitoring across two outpatient clinics. Over the last week, the care dashboard has been generating delayed and sometimes contradictory risk alerts for several patients wearing glucose patches and activity trackers, especially during morning medication hours. The meeting is between the clinical operations lead and the edge-platform engineer to diagnose why the 'real-time' soft-computing decision support model is behaving inconsistently after a recent fog-node rollout. The agenda is to compare what they each see as the main symptom, narrow likely root causes, and agree on a practical fix to stabilize alert behavior before the next clinic day. The expected outcome is a shared troubleshooting plan covering what to inspect today, what to patch this week, and what evidence will count as the issue being resolved.

members.name: Dr. Maya Srinivasan
members.expertise: Remote patient monitoring workflows, diabetes triage protocols, clinical safety review
members.background: An internist who moved into digital care operations and now oversees how algorithmic alerts are interpreted by nurses across the pilot clinics.
members.private_state: She wants the alert stream stable enough that nurses stop calling the system unreliable, but she also wants to avoid escalating the issue as a clinical safety event unless there is unmistakable evidence.
hidden_assumptions: When people say the system should work in 'real time,' they mean the alert should appear in the nurse dashboard within roughly one patient-check cycle, about 1-2 minutes from sensor capture.
The problematic 'morning spike cases' are the patients discussed in Monday's clinical huddle, where several alerts appeared after insulin had already been administered.
If the team agrees to 'replay yesterday's data,' that means replaying the exact patient-facing sequence as nurses saw it, including gateway buffering and message arrival timing.
A fix is successful if the dashboard stops producing clinically confusing sequences, even if some backend timestamps still look irregular.
The current pilot workflow already assumes that fog nodes are part of production behavior, so troubleshooting should preserve bedside responsiveness rather than fall back to cloud-only processing.

members.name: Leo Martinez
members.expertise: IoT ingestion pipelines, fog/cloud orchestration, event-stream reliability and model serving
members.background: A systems engineer who led the recent deployment of on-site fog nodes to reduce latency for wearable sensor processing in the diabetes monitoring platform.
members.private_state: He wants to show that the new fog rollout is fundamentally sound and that the issue is likely a replayable synchronization bug rather than a broader architecture problem that would force rollback.
hidden_assumptions: When people say 'real time,' they mean model inference is computed within the engineering service-level target of under 30 seconds from packet arrival at the fog node.
The relevant 'morning spike cases' are the packet bursts visible in Tuesday's infrastructure logs after one clinic gateway reconnected from a weak Wi-Fi interval.
If the team agrees to 'replay yesterday's data,' that means taking the stored normalized event stream from Kafka and rerunning inference in timestamp order, independent of original transport jitter.
A fix is successful if duplicate or stale event processing is removed and alert generation becomes internally consistent according to system timestamps.
The pilot can temporarily lean on cloud-side reconciliation without materially changing clinical behavior, because nurses mainly care that the final risk state settles correctly.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They both say the issue is that the system is not behaving 'in real time.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means nurses should see a usable alert quickly enough to affect immediate medication and triage actions, roughly within 1-2 minutes of the patient's actual physiological change.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the inference service should produce an output within the engineering latency budget after data reaches the fog node, regardless of upstream buffering or dashboard rendering lag.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both meanings are plausible and professionally standard in their own contexts, so the phrase sounds fully aligned and neither expects the other to be using a different operational clock.

misalignment_points.topic: Which 'morning spike cases' are under discussion
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both refer to 'the morning spike cases' and 'the cases from earlier this week.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking of three named patient incidents reviewed in Monday's clinical huddle, where alerts arrived after care actions had already been taken.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of Tuesday's telemetry burst pattern from one clinic gateway, visible in infrastructure logs as a cluster of delayed packets that triggered backfilled inferences.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both sets of events happened in the same general time window and produced similar symptoms, so shorthand references to 'those morning cases' feel sufficient and never get pinned to exact dates or IDs.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as 'replaying yesterday' for diagnosis
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to 'replay yesterday's data and see if the issue reproduces.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 expects a replay that preserves the original end-to-end clinical experience, including sensor delays, gateway buffering, and the order nurses saw alerts on the dashboard.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 expects a clean technical replay from the persisted normalized stream, using canonical timestamps and bypassing transport irregularities to isolate model and deduplication behavior.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Replay is a common troubleshooting verb, and each side assumes the obvious purpose of replay is the one relevant to the problem; neither sees a need to unpack implementation details in a short meeting.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree on putting in a 'temporary fix for this week.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes the temporary fix includes anything needed for clinic-facing stability this week, including suppressing confusing duplicate alerts, preserving visible responsiveness, and adjusting dashboard behavior if necessary.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes the temporary fix is limited to backend event handling around fog-node synchronization and deduplication, with any UI or workflow accommodations considered outside this troubleshooting action.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Temporary fix sounds intentionally broad and pragmatic; because both want a short-term stabilization, the phrase creates false consensus without forcing explicit boundary-setting.

If we can stabilize what they see tomorrow, I can keep this from becoming a formal clinical safety incident.
